questions.question: In Shamir secret sharing with threshold t, what is guaranteed to be information-theoretically hidden?
options: Any t shares reveal nothing about the secret
Any t+1 shares reveal nothing about the secret
Any single share reveals the secret
Any n-1 shares reveal nothing about the secret
questions.explanation: Shamir sharing is t-private: any set of at most t shares is consistent with any secret in the field.

questions.question: If a secret is shared by a degree-t polynomial f(x) and another by degree-t polynomial g(x), what is the degree of h(x)=f(x)·g(x)?
options: t
2t
questions.explanation: Multiplying two degree-t polynomials yields a degree-2t polynomial.

questions.question: Why does BGW-style MPC usually evaluate arithmetic circuits over a finite field F_p rather than over integers?
options: Because modular arithmetic provides inverses needed for interpolation
Because integers are not additive, only multiplicative
Because fields prevent any information leakage by themselves
Because Shamir sharing requires floating point arithmetic
questions.explanation: Reconstruction uses Lagrange interpolation, which requires dividing by (xj−xi); that needs multiplicative inverses in a field.

questions.question: In Shamir-based MPC, why can parties compute shares of (a+b) without any communication?
options: Addition of polynomials preserves the sharing degree and is done pointwise
Because addition is always public in MPC
Because each party can reconstruct a and b locally first
Because the dealer sends the sum directly to everyone
questions.explanation: If a is f(0) and b is g(0), then a+b is (f+g)(0); each party can add its points f(i)+g(i).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the BGW degree-reduction step after multiplying shares?
options: Convert a degree-2t sharing of ab into a fresh degree-t sharing of ab
Convert a degree-t sharing of ab into a degree-2t sharing of ab
Reveal ab to all parties so they can re-share it
Remove the need for any randomness in future gates
questions.explanation: Local multiplication raises the polynomial degree; degree reduction refreshes the sharing back to degree t without revealing the secret.

questions.question: For the passive (semi-honest) BGW multiplication described in this lesson, which condition is needed to reconstruct the degree-2t polynomial at x=0 during degree reduction?
options: n ≥ t+1
questions.explanation: A degree-2t polynomial is determined by 2t+1 points, so the protocol needs at least 2t+1 parties/points for that step.

questions.question: In degree reduction, the public coefficients λ_i are chosen so that for any degree-2t polynomial h, which relation holds?
options: h(0) = Σ_i λ_i · h(i)
h(i) = Σ_j λ_j · h(j) for all i
h(0) = Π_i h(i)
h(i) = λ_i · h(0) for all i
questions.explanation: The λ_i are Lagrange interpolation weights for evaluating the polynomial at x=0 from its values at the chosen x-coordinates.

questions.question: Attack thinking: what can go wrong if an implementation reuses the same Shamir-sharing polynomial coefficients (the same randomness) across two different secrets?
options: Shares can become correlated, enabling information leakage across secrets
Nothing; Shamir sharing is secure even with reused randomness
It only affects performance, not privacy
It only affects correctness, not privacy
questions.explanation: Reusing the same random coefficients links shares across secrets; adversaries can exploit correlations (e.g., differences cancel randomness) to learn information.
